AI-assisted, human-reviewed This is an AI-powered development project. Money we should spend — budgeted but unspent operating funds. Why haven't we spent it? — budget-vs-actual variance with context. docs.text: AI Contribution Guide ¶ The authoritative contribution guide lives at the repository root in CONTRIBUTING.md so GitHub surfaces it on PRs. It is embedded below verbatim so the docs site and the repo never drift. Contributing to the ASF Financial Dashboard (AI-Assisted Development Guide) ¶ This repository is an AI-powered development project for an Apache Software Foundation (ASF) effort. Most code and documentation here is produced with the help of generative AI tooling, driven by a structured, reviewable prompt system . This guide explains how we work and — critically — how we stay compliant with ASF policy while doing it. If you are a human directing an AI tool, you are the contributor and you carry every obligation below. If you are an AI agent reading this as context, treat it as binding operating instructions for this repository. 1. Ground rules (read this first) ¶ A human is always the contributor. AI is a tool, not an author. Every change is reviewed, understood, and vouched for by a named human before it lands. Prompts alone do not create authorship or absolve responsibility. Everything is reviewable. The prompt that produced a change is committed alongside the change (see the numbered prompt system ). Reviewers can see what was asked as well as what was produced . Disclose AI involvement in commit messages using a provenance token (see §3 ). Documentation-first. This project's functional priorities are extensibility and ease of use, and it is documentation-first. A change that isn't documented isn't done. When in doubt about licensing or provenance, stop and ask. Email legal-private@apache.org or raise it with the project lead rather than guessing. 2. How we build: the two-layer prompt workflow ¶ Development is driven by prompts, organized in two layers: Meta-prompt ──generates──▶ Numbered prompts ──drive──▶ Code / docs / design (the "how to (00-, 01-, 02- … (reviewed, tested, ask" template) executed in order) committed by a human) Layer 1 — the meta-prompt is a template that generates prompts . It encodes what we know about the project (architecture, constraints, financial structure, stakeholders) and a reusable structure for producing good, specific prompts. It lives at prompts/asf-financial-dashboard-requirements.md . Layer 2 — numbered prompts are the concrete, ordered instructions that actually build the dashboard. They are generated with the help of the meta-prompt, refined by a human, then executed in sequence. See §5 and §4 for the details of each. 3. ASF generative AI policy compliance ¶ This is the non-negotiable part. It implements the ASF's Generative Tooling Guidance . Read that page; this section summarizes your obligations for this repo. 3.1 Your ICLA obligations still apply ¶ When you contribute AI-assisted work you are still bound by the Apache Individual Contributor License Agreement (ICLA): Section 4 — you must be entitled to grant the license. That entitlement depends on your AI tool's terms of use: they must grant you ownership of (or rights broad enough to contribute) the output under Apache-2.0, and must not restrict the output in a way inconsistent with the Open Source Definition . Find the clause in your provider's ToU that addresses ownership/use of output and confirm it before contributing. Section 5 — you represent the work is your original creation. A contribution simultaneously (a) discloses any third-party material it contains and (b) states the rest is your own work. Both must hold for AI-assisted work. Section 7 (not a practical route for AI). Section 7 covers submitting work that is not your original creation, but it requires the complete details of the work's source. For AI output those details are generally unknowable, so do not rely on Section 7 to launder AI-generated material into a contribution. Section 8 — ongoing duty to notify. If you later learn something that makes your representations inaccurate (e.g. the output reproduced incompatibly licensed code), you must tell the Foundation: legal-private@apache.org . 3.2 The two conditions every AI contribution must meet ¶ Per the guidance, AI-generated code/docs may be contributed only if both : Condition 1 — tooling terms are compatible. The tool's ToU grant you sufficient rights in the output and impose no OSD-inconsistent restrictions (see §3.1, Section 4). Condition 2 — at least ONE of the following is true: # Condition Notes 2.1 The output is not copyrightable subject matter (and wouldn't be even if a human produced it). Legally unsettled — do not lean on this alone. 2.2 No third-party materials are included in the output. Preferred route. 2.3 Any third-party materials are used with permission (compatible OSS license) and in compliance with that license. Preferred route; follow the 3rd Party Licensing Policy . Prefer 2.2 or 2.3. Relying on 2.1 alone ties the contribution to a legal question nobody has answered yet. Where practical, establish that the output contains no third-party material, or only properly-licensed third-party material. Condition 3 — reasonable certainty. You gain reasonable certainty that 2.2 or 2.3 holds when the tool reports similarity to its training data, or from code scanning results. Many tools report nothing and scanners only match known OSS, so this certainty is not always achievable — when it isn't, say so in review and treat the change with extra caution (prefer small, well-understood diffs). 3.3 Commit provenance (required) ¶ Every commit containing AI-assisted content must disclose the tool in the commit message trailer, using one of: Generated-by: <Tool Name> <Version> or, when the human meaningfully co-authored the result: Co-authored-by: <Tool Name> <Version> Examples: Generated-by: Claude (Anthropic) opus-4.x Co-authored-by: GitHub Copilot 2026.10 This feeds a future machine-parsable Tooling-Provenance file, so keep the token format exact. If a commit also closes a numbered prompt, reference it: Prompt: 03-core-app-skeleton.md . 3.4 Documentation and images ¶ The same rules apply to documentation and images . Watch for tools whose generated-content licensing is restrictive, and confirm compliance with the 3rd Party Licensing Policy and 3rd Party Works . 3.5 Publishing publicly (EU AI Act) ¶ Different rules apply to AI-generated text published to the public — project announcements, release notes, blog posts, security advisories, and this project's docs website . Under the EU AI Act (in force since 2 August 2026), such text must be labeled as AI-generated unless a person reviewed it before publication and takes responsibility for it. For us that means: a committer/PMC member reviews the docs site content before it publishes (normal review, nothing extra). If content is ever published without human review — e.g. a bot auto-posting — it must carry a clear AI-generated label. In short: review it before you publish it, or label it. Our docs are built locally from the default branch after human-reviewed merges — source in docs-src/ , built HTML committed to docs/ and served by GitHub Pages ( /docs , no CI) — which satisfies the review path. 3.6 Tool choice ¶ The ASF does not maintain an approved-tools list and does not tell you which tool to use. Use whatever you like provided you follow this guidance . Don't second-guess a vendor's terms of use — your usage is bound by the totality of their ToU and you are not expected to look outside that text. 4. The numbered prompt system ¶ Numbered prompts are the ordered, concrete instructions that build the project. They live in prompts/ and follow a strict convention so the build is reproducible and auditable. 4.1 Naming ¶ prompts/NN-short-kebab-slug.md NN — zero-padded, two-digit sequence number ( 00 , 01 , …, 10 , …). Numbers define execution order , not priority. short-kebab-slug — a terse description, e.g. 03-core-app-skeleton . 00 is reserved for context/baseline (the shared project state every later prompt assumes). See prompts/00-context.md . Reserve ranges to keep things navigable (adjust as the project grows): Range Theme 00 Context / baseline 01–09 Requirements & design 10–29 Core application & plugin framework 30–59 Plugins (data sources, storage, metrics, forecasting, reports, MCP) 60–79 UI / dashboard 80–89 Testing, CI, deployment 90–99 Docs, polish, release 4.2 Anatomy of a prompt ¶ Every numbered prompt uses this front-matter + body so it is self-describing and reviewable: --- id: 03-core-app-skeleton status: draft # draft | ready | executed | superseded depends_on: [00-context, 02-architecture] produces: [app/, pyproject.toml] model: claude-sonnet-4.5 # tool/model this prompt is intended for provenance: Generated-by: Claude (Anthropic) sonnet-4.x --- # 03 — Core App Skeleton ## Goal One sentence: what this prompt should accomplish. ## Inputs - Which prior outputs / files this prompt assumes (link them). ## Tasks 1. Explicit, ordered steps for the agent. 2. … ## Outputs - Exact files/dirs expected, and acceptance criteria. ## Verification - How a human confirms the output is correct (tests to run, what to eyeball). ## Provenance & licensing notes - Expected third-party deps and their licenses; any §3.2 condition relied on. 4.3 Lifecycle of a prompt ¶ Generate a draft with help from the meta-prompt (§5). Refine it with a human — tighten scope, add acceptance criteria, pin the model, note expected dependencies and their licenses. Mark ready . Execute it with the chosen AI tool. Review the output: read it, run the verification steps, check §3.2 conditions, confirm no unexpected third-party material. Commit the resulting change and flip the prompt's status: executed , with a provenance trailer (§3.3) and Prompt: NN-slug.md . If a later decision invalidates a prompt, mark it superseded (never delete — history is the audit trail) and add the replacement with a new number. 4.4 The prompt index ¶ prompts/README.md is the human-readable index of every numbered prompt, its status, and what it produced. Keep it current — it is the map of how the dashboard was built. 5. The meta-prompt process ¶ The meta-prompt ( prompts/asf-financial-dashboard-requirements.md ) is a template for generating prompts , not a prompt that builds code directly. It captures the project's known state and a reusable structure so every generated prompt is specific, grounded, and consistent. The refinement loop: Generate an initial prompt from the meta-prompt template for a specific stakeholder or build task. Review with the technical lead: does it match scope, constraints, and the plugin architecture? Refine the questions/tasks based on feasibility. Use it — send to a stakeholder (requirements prompts) or hand to an AI tool (build prompts). Capture answers/output in structured markdown. Synthesize into the requirements doc or the next numbered prompt. Iterate — resolve conflicts, fill gaps, prioritize. Requirements-gathering prompts and build prompts both come out of this process; the former feed design, the latter feed implementation. 6. Contribution checklist ¶ Before you open a pull request: [ ] The change traces back to a numbered prompt (new or existing), and that prompt is committed/updated with status: executed . [ ] You read and understood every line of AI-generated output — you can explain and defend it in review. [ ] Verification steps ran clean (tests pass, build works, docs render). [ ] §3.2 Condition 1 (tool ToU) is satisfied for the tool you used. [ ] §3.2 Condition 2 holds (prefer 2.2 / 2.3) — no unexpected third-party material, or it's compatibly licensed and noted. [ ] Commit message carries a Generated-by: / Co-authored-by: provenance trailer and a Prompt: NN-slug.md reference. [ ] New third-party dependencies are license-checked against the 3rd Party Licensing Policy and pinned to exact versions. [ ] Public-facing text (docs, announcements) is human-reviewed before it publishes (§3.5). [ ] Documentation updated (this is a documentation-first project). 7. Pull requests & commits ¶ Branch from the default branch; name branches descriptively. Keep PRs small and tied to one prompt where possible — small diffs are easier to review and to establish provenance for. One logical change per commit; include the provenance and prompt trailers. The default branch is protected: changes land via reviewed PRs, which is also our EU AI Act review gate (§3.5). 8. Project facts (quick reference) ¶ Stack: Python + Quart (async) + Jinja2 + Bootstrap 5; uv + pyproject.toml . Architecture: plugin-based — drop-in .py files in plugins/ inheriting base classes; the core must be extensible without modification. Storage: plugin (SQLite default; PostgreSQL optional). Deployment: ASF-hosted Ubuntu LTS, systemd + Apache httpd; ASF LDAP auth eventually. Financial scope: ~$4M total (~$2M restricted reserve, ~$2M operating cash); committee-level budgets; configurable fiscal year. Finance details (categories, thresholds, fiscal dates) require a finance stakeholder — do not invent them; gather them via requirements prompts. This guide is itself a living, AI-assisted document. It was drafted with generative tooling and is human-reviewed before publication, per §3.5.

docs.text: Policy Compliance ¶ This project follows the ASF Generative Tooling Guidance . The full obligations are in AI Contribution Guide §3 ; this page is the fast checklist. Read the guide — this is a reminder, not a substitute. Every AI-assisted contribution must ¶ [ ] Have a human contributor who read and understood the output and can defend it in review. Prompts do not create authorship. [ ] Satisfy your ICLA obligations — you are entitled to grant the license (ICLA §4), the work is your original creation / third-party material is disclosed (§5), and you will notify legal-private@apache.org if a representation later proves inaccurate (§8). Do not route AI output through §7. [ ] Meet Condition 1 — the AI tool's terms of use grant you sufficient rights in the output and impose no restrictions inconsistent with the Open Source Definition . [ ] Meet Condition 2 — at least one of: 2.1 output is not copyrightable (legally unsettled — don't rely on alone) 2.2 no third-party material (preferred) 2.3 third-party material is compatibly licensed and compliant (preferred) [ ] Disclose provenance in the commit trailer: Generated-by: <Tool> <Version> or Co-authored-by: <Tool> <Version> . [ ] License-check dependencies against the 3rd Party Licensing Policy and record them in the SBOM . [ ] Human-review before public publication (EU AI Act): this docs site and any announcement/release note must be reviewed by a committer/PMC member before it publishes, or carry a clear AI-generated label. How this repo satisfies the publishing rule ¶ The docs site is built locally from the default branch after human-reviewed merges — source in docs-src/ , built HTML committed to docs/ and served by GitHub Pages ( /docs , no CI). The reviewer who merges takes responsibility for the published text, which is exactly what the EU AI Act path requires — no extra labeling is needed as long as the review gate holds. If content is ever auto-published without review, it must be labeled AI-generated. Tooling ¶ The ASF maintains no approved-tools list — use any tool that lets you meet the above. Don't second-guess a vendor's terms of use; your usage is bound by the totality of their ToU.

Prompt System ¶ Development is driven by prompts organized in two layers. The full, binding description is in the AI Contribution Guide ; this page is the overview. flowchart LR A["Meta-prompt
(template for asking well)"] -->|generates| B["Numbered prompts
00-, 01-, 02- …"] B -->|drive| C["Code · Docs · Design"] C -->|reviewed & committed by a human| D["Repository"] D -->|learnings update| A Layer 1 — the meta-prompt ¶ prompts/asf-financial-dashboard-requirements.md is a template that generates prompts , not a prompt that builds code. It encodes what we know (architecture, constraints, financial structure, stakeholders) plus a reusable structure for producing specific, grounded prompts. The refinement loop: generate → review with the lead → refine → use → capture → synthesize → iterate. It produces both requirements-gathering prompts (which feed design) and build prompts (which feed implementation). Layer 2 — numbered prompts ¶ Concrete, ordered instructions named NN-short-kebab-slug.md , where NN is the zero-padded execution order. 00 is the shared context baseline. Range Theme 00 Context / baseline 01–09 Requirements & design 10–29 Core application & plugin framework 30–59 Plugins 60–79 UI / dashboard 80–89 Testing, CI, deployment 90–99 Docs, polish, release Each prompt carries front-matter ( id , status , depends_on , produces , model , provenance ) and a body of Goal / Inputs / Tasks / Outputs / Verification / Provenance notes . Lifecycle: draft → ready → executed , or superseded (never deleted — history is the audit trail). We are not pre-authoring the build prompts Only the context baseline ( prompts/00-context.md ) exists today. Numbered build prompts are created as the work reaches them, each reviewed and refined before execution. The index in prompts/README.md tracks them as they appear.

docs.text: Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) ¶ A living inventory of every third-party dependency this project ships or builds with, plus its license. This matters for two reasons: ASF 3rd-party licensing policy — every dependency must be compatible with Apache-2.0 per the 3rd Party Licensing Policy . Category X licenses must not be included; Category B has conditions. AI provenance — AI-generated code can silently pull in dependencies. Tracking them here is part of satisfying Contribution Guide §3.2 (no unexpected third-party material, or compatibly licensed and disclosed). Scope today The application is not built yet, so the only actual dependencies are the documentation toolchain. The runtime rows are the planned stack and are marked accordingly — they become real (with pinned versions) as the numbered prompts implement them. Documentation toolchain (in use) ¶ Component Version License Category Purpose mkdocs >=1.6 BSD-2-Clause A Static docs site generator pymdown-extensions >=10.0 MIT A Markdown extensions (snippets, superfences, mermaid) Pygments >=2.17 BSD-2-Clause A Code-block syntax highlighting The docs use a custom MkDocs theme built on Bootstrap 5 (in theme/ , Jinja2 templates — matching the dashboard's own stack), not a third-party theme package. These front-end assets load client-side from a CDN at page-view time (not build dependencies): Asset Version License Category Purpose Bootstrap 5.3.3 MIT A CSS/JS framework Bootstrap Icons 1.11.3 MIT A Icon font Mermaid 10.x MIT A Client-side diagram rendering Planned runtime stack (not yet built) ¶ Component Intended version License Category Purpose Python 3.12+ PSF A Language runtime Quart TBD MIT A Async web framework Jinja2 TBD BSD-3-Clause A Templating Bootstrap 5.x MIT A Frontend CSS/JS SQLite (via stdlib sqlite3 ) stdlib Public Domain A Default storage backend PostgreSQL driver (optional) TBD TBD TBD Optional storage backend — vet before adding Category refers to the ASF classification: A = compatible, B = allowed with conditions, X = prohibited. Confirm each row against the policy before a dependency lands; do not treat this table as a legal sign-off. Keeping this current ¶ Pin exact versions in pyproject.toml / docs/requirements.txt when a dependency becomes real, then reflect them here. When the app exists, generate a machine-readable SBOM in CI — e.g. CycloneDX via cyclonedx-py — and link the artifact from this page. A generated SBOM supplements, but does not replace, the human license-category review required by ASF policy. Any dependency introduced by AI-generated code must be added here as part of the same PR (Contribution Guide checklist).
